taxonomyNotes: Millepora Linnaeus, 1758 is a hydrocoral (Cnidaria: Hydrozoa: Anthoathecata: Milleporidae; WoRMS AphiaID 205902), not a scleractinian stony coral. The trade name 'fire coral' covers several species whose growth forms overlap (blades: M. complanata, M. platyphylla; branching: M. alcicornis, M. tenera, M. dichotoma), so the asset carries a genus-level label and models the two habits as variants.

referenceSize.note: Branching Millepora alcicornis colonies reach about 50 cm tall in sheltered water and M. platyphylla plates exceed a metre across (Razak & Hoeksema 2003; Lewis 2006 via WoRMS/Wikipedia). 15 cm is the width, dactylozooids extended, of a small aquarium colony, which is what this candidate depicts. Gastropores measure 0.15 to 0.36 mm and dactylopores 0.06 to 0.24 mm (de Weerdt 1981; Ruiz-Ramos et al. 2014); at this scale they are sub-texel and are painted as cyclosystem speckle rather than modelled.

morphology.notes: Smooth calcareous coenosteum without corallites, pierced by minute pores (painted). Blade form: upright wavy plates with lobed pale upper margins on an encrusting base. Branching form: stout laterally compressed stems forking dichotomously into blunt pale-tipped branchlets. Hair-like dactylozooids protrude everywhere from the tissue-covered surface.

visualDebt: Dactylozooids are drawn about twice their real diameter (0.28 mm radius) and at a fraction of their real density so they read at LOD1; real colonies carry thousands of finer hairs per square centimetre.
Gastropores and dactylopores are painted as cyclosystem speckle in the albedo and normal maps, not modelled as holes.

Hairs in one cluster share a bone: bending comes from root-to-tip weight blending plus baked per-hair lean and gain, so hairs within a cluster move in step with a small twist gradient; hair-vs-hair clearance is not proven.

Branching form: dichotomous forks are fused intersecting tubes (parent knuckle plus two children) rather than a single smoothed junction; sibling branches are not clearance-checked against each other at the fork.
Blade form: blades are separate lofts that root in the encrusting base and do not fuse into the honeycomb plates seen in M. platyphylla.
